Omnilogue is an open‑source desktop application with an optional self‑hosted WebUI that lets you browse, search, and analyze the history of many AI coding assistants while keeping all data local.

🔍 Overview

  • Desktop app and web server to browse, search and analyze AI coding assistant history — Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode and more.
  • 100 % offline; the app reads conversation files on disk and does not upload session data or require an Omnilogue account.
  • Supports a long list of assistants, including Aider, Amazon Q CLI, Antigravity, Claude Code, Cline, CodeBuddy, Codex CLI, Continue.dev, Cursor, ForgeCode, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, OpenHands, PearAI, Pi, Qoder, Qwen Code, Zed, and many others.

🧩 How it works

  • The desktop app reads local conversation files; an optional server can be run on the same machine for browser access.
  • Example server binds to loopback only and is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:3727.
  • Server guide covers prebuilt binaries, Docker, and authentication for network access.
  • Technical requirements: Node.js 20.19+ (or 22.12+), pnpm, and a stable Rust toolchain. Linux build prerequisites are listed in the Linux guide.
  • Build the desktop bundle with pnpm tauri:build.

⚙️ Key details

  • Platforms: macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows x64, Linux x86‑64.
  • Installation: desktop download for each platform; macOS Homebrew support; Flatpak and other Linux packages via the Linux guide.
  • Updates: existing installs can update in place while keeping favorites and settings.
  • Usage insights: review tokens and estimated API costs where logs provide data; separate visibility into sub‑agent work.
  • Session navigation: find conversations again, browse by project or assistant, search across sessions, follow conversation branches, jump between steps, and inspect tool calls and file edits.

🚀 Availability

  • Download links are provided for each supported OS.
  • macOS users may also install via Homebrew.
  • Linux users can use Flatpak or follow the Linux guide for other package managers.
  • The optional WebUI server can be run locally; see the server guide for details.

💡 Why it matters

  • Keeps AI coding assistant history fully local, protecting privacy and avoiding external accounts.
  • Independent project, not affiliated with any of the assistants whose history it reads, offering a neutral tool for developers to review their own AI‑assisted work.

#Omnilogue #AIHistory #OpenSource

item.title: Pydantic AI Skills Enhances Agent Capabilities with Progressive Disclosure
item.description:
Pydantic AI Skills Enhances Agent Capabilities with Progressive Disclosure

Pydantic AI Skills introduces enhanced capabilities for Agent Skills, supporting progressive disclosure and modular packages of instructions, resources, and scripts. This update allows agents to handle specialized tasks more efficiently by loading only the necessary resources when needed.

🔍 Overview

  • Pydantic AI Skills enhances Agent Skills with progressive disclosure.
  • Supports filesystem and programmatic skills.
  • Enables remote skill registries and bundled-file execution.

🧩 How it works

  • Agent Skills are modular packages of instructions, resources, and scripts.
  • On disk, a skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file, reference documents, and executable scripts.
  • Your agent starts with only the name and description of each skill.
  • When a task calls for a skill, it loads the full instructions and resources only if needed.
  • This is progressive disclosure, allowing the skill library to grow without every skill paying for space in the prompt.

⚙️ Key details

  • pydantic-ai-harness ships a Skills capability that reads SKILL.md packages from local directories.
  • pydantic-ai-skills is the companion that fills the gaps, including remote registries and bundled-file execution.
  • Remote registries support Git and S3 sources, with composition features.
  • Bundled files can be read or executed with read_skill_resource and run_skill_script.
  • Sandboxed execution keeps untrusted scripts off the host.
  • ${SKILL_DIR} resolution substitutes the path in scripts.
  • Programmatic skills can be defined in Python within the same catalog.
  • v2 introduces SkillsToolset, SkillsDirectory, reload(), and tools for listing and loading skills.
  • Each skill becomes its own deferred capability, with names and descriptions acting as fields the runtime uses.

💡 Why it matters

  • Progressive disclosure allows the skill library to grow without every skill paying for space in the prompt.
  • Enhanced capabilities for handling specialized tasks more efficiently.
  • Supports remote skill registries and bundled-file execution.
  • Sandboxed execution ensures security for untrusted scripts.

#PydanticAI #AgentSkills #ProgressiveDisclosure #AIAgents #AITools

Source: DougTrajano/pydantic-ai-skills

item.title: RTK CLI Proxy Compresses Developer Command Outputs to Reduce AI Token Costs by 60-90%
item.description:
RTK CLI Proxy Compresses Developer Command Outputs to Reduce AI Token Costs by 60-90%

RTK is a new CLI proxy designed as a cost reduction engine for AI coding agents, reducing LLM token consumption by 60% to 90% on common development commands. Built as a single Rust binary with zero dependencies, the tool operates under 25 milliseconds per command across over 100 commands without changing how you work.

🔍 Overview

RTK acts as a command-line intermediary that compresses test runs, diffs, logs, and builds before they are read by an AI agent. For instance, when an agent runs git status, RTK runs rtk git status and delivers a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. This allows developers to clean API traffic and reduce token volume without breaking prompt caching. The tool has already seen adoption by developers at Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Apple, NVIDIA, IBM, Tencent, ByteDance, Alibaba, Shopify, Datadog, SAP, Adobe, Intel, Samsung, Bosch, Cisco, JPMorgan Chase, Oracle, Netflix, Toyota, Salesforce, Siemens, Accenture, Uber, Spotify, and over 1,100 other companies.

🧩 How it works

RTK handles command compression and optimization through several primary mechanisms:

  • Output Compression: Trims and compresses terminal outputs by up to 90% to prevent agents from processing redundant logs.
  • Heavy Read Delegation: Allows developers to hand off heavy reads to a cheaper model.
  • Agent-Agnostic Pipelines: Uses a single configuration file that allows developers to use built-in pipelines, install shared pipelines, or write and share custom pipelines. The top community pipeline reduces total cost by 20.2% in benchmark runs.
  • RTK Pro: Serves as a control layer for AI agents, functioning as a single gateway for AI calls, costs, secrets, personal data, policies, team catalogs, and audit logs.

⚙️ Tracking savings

Every command managed by RTK is counted locally on your machine. You can view your saved tokens and performance metrics using the following tracking commands:

Command Action
rtk gain Displays summary statistics of saved tokens
rtk gain --graph Displays an ASCII graph of savings over the last 30 days
rtk gain --history Displays your recent command history
rtk gain --daily Displays a day-by-day breakdown of savings
rtk gain --all --format json Exports your savings data in JSON format for dashboards

🚀 Availability

RTK can be installed on your machine using one of the following methods:

  • Homebrew (macOS): 
    1

    brew install rtk
  • Winget (Windows): 
    1

    winget install rtk-ai.rtk
  • Shell Script: 
    1

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh

To initialize the proxy for Claude Code and other agents, run the hook registration command:

1

rtk init -g

#rtk #AIagents #LLM #DeveloperTools #Rust

item.title: Simple Python bindings for llama.cpp released
item.description:
Simple Python bindings for llama.cpp released

Simple Python bindings for the llama.cpp library are now available, providing low-level access to the C API via ctypes and a high-level Python API for text completion.

🧩 How it works

The package allows developers to integrate llama.cpp into Python environments with several key interfaces:

  • Low-level access: Direct access to the C API through a ctypes interface.
  • High-level API: A Python API designed for text completion.
  • OpenAI-like API: Compatibility with standard OpenAI-style interfaces.
  • Framework Support: Includes compatibility with LangChain and LlamaIndex.
  • Web Server: Features an OpenAI compatible web server.

⚙️ Key details

The server component supports a range of additional capabilities, including:

  • Function Calling support
  • Vision API support for multimodal models
  • Configuration and multi-model support
  • Local Copilot replacement for code completion

Installation requires Python 3.8+ and a C compiler. The build process compiles llama.cpp from source and installs it alongside the Python package. Hardware acceleration backends are supported via specific environment variables:

  • OpenBLAS: Set GGML_BLAS and GGML_BLAS_VENDOR.
  • CUDA: Set GGML_CUDA=on. Supported CUDA versions include 11.8, 12.1, 12.2, 12.3, 12.4, 12.5, 13.0, or 13.2. GPU compute capability requirements vary by version: 6.0–8.9 for CUDA 11.8, 6.0+ for CUDA 12, and 7.5+ for CUDA 13. Pre-built wheels for CUDA support Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12.
  • Metal (MPS): Set GGML_METAL=on. Requires macOS 11.0 or later.

All llama.cpp cmake build options can be configured via the CMAKE_ARGS environment variable or the --config-settings / -C CLI flag during installation.

🚀 Availability

Documentation is available at https://llama-cpp-python.readthedocs.io/en/latest. Installation is supported on Linux (gcc or clang), Windows (Visual Studio or MinGW), and MacOS (Xcode).

item.title: Updates on Production-Grade Microservice Boilerplates and Wazuh Security Platform
item.description:
Updates on Production-Grade Microservice Boilerplates and Wazuh Security Platform

Recent developments highlight updates regarding a production-grade microservice boilerplate and the features of the Wazuh open-source security platform.

🔍 Overview

A production-grade microservice boilerplate has been introduced, featuring tools such as GORM, Goose, Swag, Zerolog, Validator.v10, GitOps, Kubernetes, Kustomize, ArgoCD, and Istio. Additionally, Wazuh continues to serve as a free and open-source platform used for threat prevention, detection, and response across on-premises, virtualized, containerized, and cloud-based environments.

⚙️ Key details

  • The microservice boilerplate builds a production-ready containerized RESTful API server application using Go standard library net/http and the Chi router.
  • Development environments use golang:1.27-alpine (~1180 MB) and postgres:19-alpine (~440 MB), while production uses distroless/static-debian13:nonroot (~46 MB).
  • For high-traffic systems with large PostgreSQL tables, arranging fixed-width columns by decreasing alignment requirements can reduce tuple alignment padding and potentially minimize storage size, a technique called “Column Tetris”.
  • Wazuh’s architecture consists of an endpoint security agent and a management server.
  • Wazuh agents scan monitored systems for malware, rootkits, suspicious anomalies, hidden files, cloaked processes, and unregistered network listeners.
  • The Wazuh server uses a signature-based approach to intrusion detection with a regular expression engine.
  • Wazuh provides native integration with the Docker engine to monitor images, volumes, network settings, and running containers.
  • Cloud infrastructure monitoring includes integration modules for Amazon AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

💡 Why it matters

These tools help organizations build robust containerized RESTful APIs with automated GitOps deployment via ArgoCD, while maintaining comprehensive security, threat detection, and regulatory compliance with standards such as PCI DSS, GPG13, and GDPR using Wazuh.

#Microservices #Go #Kubernetes #Security #Wazuh

item.title: Kronk Released as a Go SDK and Server for Local AI Inference
item.description:
Kronk Released as a Go SDK and Server for Local AI Inference

Kronk has been released as a Go SDK and production-ready model server designed for hardware-accelerated local inference. It allows developers to use Go to directly integrate llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, and stable-diffusion.cpp into their applications.

🔍 Overview

The Kronk model server is built on the same public SDKs that are available to Go applications. The system provides a high-level API and integrates with OpenWebUI, OpenCode, and Claude Code. It also includes features for model management, security, observability, and a browser interface.

⚙️ Key Components

The capabilities of Kronk are divided across several subsystems and SDK features:

Subsystem / Component Supported Capabilities and Features
Kronk SDK Text generation, streaming, reasoning, tool calls, vision, embeddings, reranking, typed Decision questions, buffered text-to-speech, concurrent processing, and incremental message caching.
Kronk Model Server OpenAI-compatible APIs (for Chat Completions, Responses, embeddings, reranking, and audio transcription), Anthropic-compatible Messages API, and Decision endpoints at /v1/systemone and /v1/decide.
Speech Supports Chatterbox Turbo and Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base with memory planning and typed pools across native backends. Currently SDK-only (no HTTP speech-generation endpoint or BUI speech playground).
Bucky File transcription, translation, channel-separated diarization, and live streaming transcription.
Experimental Malina Text-to-image, image-to-image, Canny ControlNet conditioning, ADetailer face refinement, AnimateDiff video generation, Real-ESRGAN upscaling, single-checkpoint and multi-file diffusion pipelines, and Motion-JPEG encoding. Currently SDK-only.

🧩 Hardware Acceleration and Dependencies

Kronk’s performance and execution model rely on several hardware and library management behaviors:

  • Automatic Downloads: The first model or SDK example that runs can download the compatible native libraries and model files automatically.
  • Library Management: Every Kronk release is bound to known-compatible library versions. Instead of mixing native libraries from unrelated releases, users should use each subsystem’s downloader. Upstream changes can require coordinated releases of Yzma, Bucky, Malina, and Kronk.
  • Acceleration Support: Hardware acceleration depends on the operating system, architecture, inference engine, and library bundle. Not every backend is available for every SDK or architecture, and non-Metal memory estimates are provisional.
  • Formula Trust: The fully qualified formula name trusts only the Kronk formula, rather than every item in the ardanlabs/kronk tap.

#Golang #Inference #LLM #DeveloperTools

item.description:
NetCoreKevin Updates Enterprise AI Assistant and SaaS Agent Platform

NetCoreKevin has introduced an update for building AI assistants and SaaS agent platforms within enterprise intranets, providing foundational features such as multi-tenancy, login authentication, permission points, audit logs, scheduled tasks, and model integration.

🔍 Overview

  • Designed for enterprise intranet AI assistant and SaaS agent platform scenarios.
  • Not a scaffold demo: includes pre-built dependencies, database migration support, login management, menus, permissions, scheduled tasks, and audit logs.
  • Containerized deployment supported via Docker Compose to spin up the frontend, backend, MySQL, Redis, and Qdrant with a single command, alongside individual Dockerfiles for frontend and backend.

🧩 Architecture and Tech Stack

  • Backend: Built on .NET 10, EF Core 10, and MySQL, split into Domain, Application, RepositorieRps, and WebApi layers with v1 and v2 API versions.
  • AI Capabilities: Integrated within Kevin/kevin.Module. Uses kevin.AI.AgentFramework based on Microsoft Agent Framework, and kevin.RAG for text splitting, vectorization, and reranking in the same process without requiring an external Python service.
  • Management Frontend: vue/kevin.web.vue built with Vue 3 and Ant Design Vue for configuring tenants, users, roles, agents, knowledge bases, skills, tasks, and API keys.
  • Modular Base: Features 25 pluggable modules (each as a csproj) registered via IModuleInitializer and IModuleConfigTasks without modifying entry files, including permissions, caching, message queues, distributed locks, SignalR, Hangfire, object storage, SMS, email, and a code generator.

⚙️ Key Features and Capabilities

  • Prompt, Model, and Parameter Configuration: Individual configuration per agent, separating chat models from vector models, with adjustable temperature and context cropping.
  • Dynamic Skill Loading: Skills combine SKILL.md with scripts (.py, .ps1, .sh), allowing creation, online editing, and activation or deactivation without recompilation.
  • RAG Knowledge Base: Uploaded documents are automatically split and written to Qdrant, with retrieval results processed by qwen3-rerank before feeding into the model.
  • Memory: Isolated in Qdrant by tenant, agent, and user dimensions, with a toggle switch on individual agents.
  • Multi-Agent Collaboration: Main agents can delegate sub-tasks to other agents.
  • Context Compression: Compresses historical messages based on configuration thresholds.
  • Web Search: Integrated with Doubao search from Volcano Engine for fetching new information.
  • Multimodal Support: Handles image understanding, speech transcription (Aliyun ASR), and text-to-image generation with automatic OSS upload.
  • Tenancy and Security: Single-database multi-tenancy using shared libraries isolated by TenantId with interface-level forced filtering; RBAC permissions across menu and API dimensions tied to roles, with a toggle for debugging via IsOpenPermission.
  • Quotas and Auditing: Monthly token quotas issued via scheduled tasks and deducted on requests; built-in audit logs, slow query alerts, and environment-specific file logging.
  • OpenAI Protocol Compatibility: Supports GET /v1/models and POST /v1/chat/completions (including stream) via endpoints compatible with clients like Cherry Studio, Dify, and custom clients using a sk- prefixed key.
  • MCP Support: App/WebApiMcp provides an MCP server, allowing configuration to wrap existing HTTP interfaces into MCP tools or connect external MCP services as agent tools.
  • Integration Ecosystem: Object storage supporting Tencent Cloud, Aliyun, and Qiniu; SMS via Tencent and Aliyun; DingTalk messages; RabbitMQ and CAP message buses; Consul service discovery; and SignalR real-time push.

Netdata provides real-time distributed observability with per-second AI anomaly detection

Netdata is a full-stack observability platform that covers infrastructure, application performance, digital experience, network performance, databases, logs, and cloud environments. The system is distributed and real-time, with its Agents collecting, storing, and analyzing data where it is generated every second.

🔍 Overview

Netdata monitors multiple layers of technology, including:

  • Infrastructure
  • Application performance monitoring (OpenTelemetry traces, service maps, RED)

🧩 How it works

The architecture relies on data staying close to where it is created, stored in independent hubs placed where they make sense. Netdata Agents collect, store, and analyze data locally per second, applying machine learning anomaly detection on every metric. Netdata Parents and Netdata Cloud then combine these data points into a single view without centralizing the data itself. Because every piece of data gets its meaning at the time of collection, dashboards build themselves and ensure every chart is correct. Every metric is scored for anomalies every second, allowing clusters of anomalies to reveal hidden dependencies and show how problems cascade across systems, networks, and applications.

  • Cost Engineering: Netdata collects everything every second and engineers the cost down to about 0.6 bytes per sample, making it unnecessary to choose what to watch.
  • Scalability: The platform scales to 100,000+ nodes.
  • Agent Accessibility: The Netdata Agent is open source.
  • Unification: Netdata Cloud unifies and correlates data from distributed hubs.

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released with New Read-Your-Writes Consistency Feature
item.description:
PostgreSQL 19 Released with New Read-Your-Writes Consistency Feature

PostgreSQL 19 has been released, arriving two months later than the typical September schedule due to a flurry of issues related to AI-reported vulnerabilities.

🔍 Overview

  • The release was delayed from September by two months.
  • The delay was attributed to addressing ongoing AI-reported vulnerability issues.
  • The author considers the release “definitely worth the wait.”

🧩 How it works

The release introduces a “read-your-writes” consistency feature for applications sending reads to standbys using the new WAIT FOR LSN command. This allows a session on a standby to wait until it has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query. This ensures the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

Example Workflow

  1. Update a record on the primary: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
  2. Get the current LSN: SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); (returns a value like 0/0306EE20).
  3. Store the LSN value (e.g., in a signed cookie).
  4. On a subsequent request, use the stored LSN on a standby: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
  5. Run the query: SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout parameter is optional. If provided, the system returns an error if the replica does not catch up within the specified time.

💡 Why it matters

This pattern ensures users see events in chronological order and maintain a consistent view across subsequent requests. Similar patterns have previously been implemented in hand-rolled solutions:

  • Wikipedia/MediaWiki: Uses a hand-rolled version against MySQL replication, saving the primary binlog position in the session and waiting for replicas to catch up before reads. MediaWiki now uses MySQL’s WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

#PostgreSQL #Database #SQL #DataConsistency #WaitForLSN

Source: PostgreSQL 19 Released

item.title: Prefect Team Offers FastMCP Framework and Gateway for Model Context Protocol
item.description:
Prefect Team Offers FastMCP Framework and Gateway for Model Context Protocol

The Prefect team has developed FastMCP, a full Model Context Protocol (MCP) application framework that connects Large Language Models (LLMs) to tools and data. To support team-wide scaling, the team also provides FastMCP Gateway, an enterprise gateway for deploying, securing, and governing MCP servers and tools.

🔍 Overview

FastMCP handles the application layer of the Model Context Protocol, simplifying what is otherwise a complex development process. Since its inception, FastMCP 1.0 was incorporated into the official MCP Python SDK in 2024. Today, FastMCP is an actively maintained standalone project downloaded a million times a day, and some version of FastMCP powers 70% of MCP servers across all languages.

🧩 How it works

FastMCP automates the tedious parts of building MCP applications and operates on three primary pillars:

Pillar Description
Servers Wrap your Python functions into MCP-compliant tools, resources, and prompts.
Clients Connect to any server with full protocol support.
Apps Give your tools interactive UIs rendered directly in the conversation.

By managing the application layer, FastMCP handles several tasks automatically:

  • Tool Declaration: Declare a tool using a Python function, and the schema, validation, and documentation are generated automatically.
  • Server Connection: Connect to a server with a URL, and FastMCP manages transport negotiation, authentication, and the protocol lifecycle.

To build a server, developers start with ordinary Python. It is recommended to add FastMCP to your project with uv. For comprehensive instructions, including verification and upgrading, see the Installation Guide.

⚙️ Key details

FastMCP and its enterprise extension offer several capabilities for developers and organizations:

  • Cross-Language Support: In addition to Python, FastMCP for TypeScript is the official counterpart, built and maintained by the same team.
  • Enterprise Scaling: FastMCP Gateway allows teams to deploy FastMCP servers from GitHub with branch previews and instant rollback, create private registries of company-wide MCPs, and secure access with SSO and tool-level RBAC.
  • Observability and Governance: FastMCP Gateway provides centralized governance, audit logs, and observability across your MCP stack, allowing teams to remix approved tools into purpose-built endpoints for teams and agents.

item.title: Scaling Agentic AI and Governance in Enterprise Systems
item.description:
Scaling Agentic AI and Governance in Enterprise Systems

Forward Deployed Engineers are tackling the challenge of industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner across large organizations. Building agents that can cooperate from the start requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable without a single framework or toolchain.

🧩 How it works

  • The agent harness acts as a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM), providing the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks.
  • Governance runs as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop, implemented via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, central agent registry, and orchestration boundary.
  • Graduated trust implements per-step autonomy levels rather than per-agent trust levels, allowing teams to start conservatively and increase autonomy based on measurable evaluation data.

⚙️ Key details

The framework implements three distinct per-step autonomy levels:

Autonomy Level Description
Level 0 (Human-in-the-loop) Every action requires explicit human approval; starting point for new agents and high-risk operations.
Level 1 (Human-on-the-loop) The agent executes autonomously but surfaces decisions for asynchronous human review for medium-risk tasks.
Level 2 (Autonomous within guardrails) The agent operates independently within strictly defined, deterministically enforced policy boundaries.

💡 Why it matters

Organizations face a fundamental governance dichotomy: development teams need freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without this balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work.

#AI #AgenticAI #EnterpriseAI #Governance #MachineLearning

Source: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers | Amazon Web Services Source: Four AI Architecture Patterns for Regulated Industries

item.title: Google Launches Gemini 4 Neon to Assist with Complex Technical Workflows
item.description:
Google Launches Gemini 4 Neon to Assist with Complex Technical Workflows

Today, Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon, bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. The model excels at multi-step instruction following and can synthesize across diverse inputs in a single 1 million-token context window to turn inputs into structured deliverables, while recording its lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

🔍 Overview

  • Pricing: Gemini 4 Neon is priced at $3 per million input tokens, $0.15 per million cached input tokens (a 95% discount), and $15 per million output tokens.
  • Context Window: Features a 1 million-token context window.
  • Cost Efficiency: At its default high thinking level, Neon pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals Index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models.

📊 Performance and Benchmarks

Gemini 4 Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and demonstrates competitive performance across various industry benchmarks:

Benchmark Score / Rank Details
Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index #3 overall (Score: 61) At its xhigh thinking level, landing behind larger, slower models
Vals Index #2 (70.9%) Lands on the Pareto frontier
Legal Research Bench #1 Reaches the top spot
Tax Agent Bench #1 Reaches the top spot
Chartography 73.5% For reading dense professional charts
Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 75.8% Performs on par with leading models
Zapier’s AutomationBench #1 overall (56.3%) Automation benchmark
Andon Labs’ Vending-Bench 2 #1 overall ($16,843) Long-horizon simulation of running a business
Agent Arena Index #2 globally (Score: 1336) Evaluated across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions
Terminal-Bench Science 70.5% Best-in-class on scientific and mathematical reasoning
RiemannBench 84.0% Best-in-class on scientific and mathematical reasoning
HLE-Diamond 71.3% Best-in-class on scientific and mathematical reasoning

💻 Developer and Cybersecurity Workflows

Neon delivers competitive results across developer, researcher, and cybersecurity-focused tests:

  • Coding Performance: Neon ranks #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6). It scores 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its default high setting.
  • SWE-sweep: The model leads on the mini-SWE harness with 12.8%, which more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% when utilized within the Google Antigravity harness.
  • AutoBaxBench: Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).
  • WebExploitBench v1.2: Achieves a state-of-the-art 51.26% at half the cost of competing large models.
  • SEC-bench Pro: Reaches a state-of-the-art 90.5% while costing roughly half as much per challenge.
  • ExploitGym: Delivers frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon.
  • CWE-bench v2: Achieves 70.7% on Collinear’s benchmark, representing a 3.4% uplift over Carbon.

🚀 Availability

Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today across the following platforms and services:

  • The Gemini API in Google AI Studio
  • Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown)
  • Paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity
  • Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app

item.title: Kernel-Enforced Sandbox Released for AI Coding Agents
item.description:
Kernel-Enforced Sandbox Released for AI Coding Agents

An update has been released regarding cplt, a kernel-enforced sandbox designed for AI coding agents to prevent credential theft, unauthorized pushes to main, PR merges, and secret exfiltration.

🔍 Overview

AI agents execute arbitrary code, and a compromised agent can read ~/.ssh, push to main, merge PRs, or exfiltrate code unless the operating system prevents it. The cplt tool acts as a kernel-level sandbox and wrapper for various AI coding interfaces and shells.

🧩 How it works

The tool wraps multiple coding agents and shells to ensure that while the agent can write code, it cannot perform restricted destructive actions or access sensitive files. Every restriction applies to the agent and to every process it spawns.

  • Runs Copilot CLI, Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Pi, goose, DeepSeek Harness, or a plain shell
  • Deny by default for credentials, secrets, and sensitive files
  • Command-level git and gh interception
  • Outbound network filtering with an audit log
  • Per-repo policy in .cplt.toml, committed to version control for tamper-proof auditing
  • Zero-config start for developers with escape hatches

⚙️ Key details

Operating system support and isolation mechanisms vary by platform:

Platform Mechanism Details
macOS Apple Seatbelt/SBPL via sandbox-exec Supported
Linux Landlock LSM + seccomp-BPF + optional Bubblewrap Kernel 5.13+, full network filtering on 6.7+
Windows No native support Run inside WSL2 (ordinary Linux install where Microsoft kernel ships Landlock)

Additional configuration and usage commands include:

  • brew install navikt/tap/cplt (macOS)
  • cplt --shell-install to make ‘copilot’ run sandboxed persistently
  • cplt doctor to check the environment
  • cplt -- -p "fix the tests" to run Copilot in the sandbox
  • cplt config set git_guard.protect_default_branch_only false to block every push instead of just main
  • cplt config set git_guard.mode warn to observe instead of blocking

🚀 Availability

  • Distributed as a single binary that runs on a locked-down laptop
  • Installation available via Homebrew for macOS (brew install navikt/tap/cplt) and via apt for Debian or Ubuntu

#AI #Security #DeveloperTools #AIAgents #Linux

Source: navikt/cplt

item.title: MimirQ Releases Version 1.0.1 to Improve Enterprise Knowledge Base Error Localization and Quality
item.description:
MimirQ Releases Version 1.0.1 to Improve Enterprise Knowledge Base Error Localization and Quality

MimirQ, an enterprise knowledge base solution originating from real-world government knowledge base deliveries, has released its latest stable version, v1.0.1. The project focuses on addressing the core challenges of long-term delivery, estimation, acceptance, and governance by ensuring that errors are locatable, strategies are replaceable, and quality is regressible throughout the pipeline.

🔍 Overview

Hiding an entire RAG pipeline behind a simple upload button may work for quick prototypes, but it makes long-term delivery difficult to estimate, accept, and govern. When answers are incorrect, teams must be able to quickly determine whether the issue originates from parsing, data governance, chunking, recall, reranking, or generation deviation from the references. MimirQ is designed to make each step of the input, output, reference tracing, and versioning auditable, using a Golden dataset of 800 fixed test questions to maintain release quality.

🛠️ Data Processing Pipeline

To handle diverse datasets, MimirQ recommends first evaluating sample data and then choosing specific parsers based on the material type:

Material Type Recommended Parsers to Evaluate
Complex layouts or scanned documents MinerU / DeepDoc
Formulas, tables, and layout-dense materials Docling
Digital native Office or plain text MarkItDown

High-risk materials still require manual verification. After parsing, results are governed using scripts, rules DSL, or plugins. They are then chunked according to titles, chapters, business records, or parent-child relationships instead of relying on uniform, fixed-length windows with overlapping sections. The default parser is the built-in DeepDoc, with other parsers started only as required by business needs.

🧩 Capabilities and Architecture

The repository features broad strategy coverage and standardizes on flexible infrastructure layers:

  • Repository Coverage: The system covers 30 parsing backends, 86 chunking strategies, and 13 classes of rerankers, with 800 questions of test evidence.
  • Index Layer: Uses vector databases like Milvus, combining BM25, vector search, and reranking.
  • Upper Application Layer: Can integrate with Dify, LangGraph, PydanticAI, or a simple API service.

⚙️ Deployment and Operation

MimirQ runs locally and manages dependencies through Docker Compose using a dedicated Compose project name mimirq to prevent conflicts with other services like Dify:

  • Initialization: Run make init to create the missing .env and web/.env.local files without overwriting existing configurations.
  • Execution: Access the platform locally at http://localhost:3000 after startup. If no administrator account is preconfigured, the first registered account on the page becomes the administrator.
  • Teardown: Run make down to stop the services. To clear persistent data, run make docker-reset, or use make docker-purge to delete the project service images as well (these latter two operations are non-recoverable).

🚀 Availability

MimirQ v1.0.1 is available now as the latest stable release. Complete guides covering model services, admin setup, data ingestion, and testing workflow are provided within the project documentation.

#MimirQ #RAG #EnterpriseKnowledge #AIv101

Source: skygazer42/MimirQ

item.title: Reactor 3 Java Reactive Library Overview and Build Requirements
item.description:
Reactor 3 Java Reactive Library Overview and Build Requirements

Reactor 3 is a non-blocking Reactive Streams foundation for the JVM, implementing a Reactive Extensions-inspired API with efficient event streaming support.

⚙️ Key details

  • Reactor 3 requires Java 8 or higher to run.
  • Reactor 3 does not officially support nor target Android.
  • However, it should work fine with Android SDK 21 (Android 5.0) and above.
  • Since 3.3.x, the repository also contains reactor-tools, a Java agent aimed at helping with debugging of Reactor code.

🧩 How it works

Reactor functions as a Reactive Streams Publisher with basic flow operators. Its architecture includes:

  • Static factories on Flux: Allow for source generation from arbitrary callback types.
  • Instance methods: Allow for operational building, materialized on each subscription (such as Flux#subscribe()), or multicasting operations (such as Flux#publish and Flux#publishNext).

🚀 Availability and Build

The build process involves specific Java Development Kit (JDK) requirements due to support for Java Multi-Release JAR Files.

Requirement Detail
Classpath JDKs JDK 8, 9, and 21 must be available.
Toolchain Management Gradle Toolchains should automatically detect or provision the required JDKs.
Active Shell JDK Must be compatible with JDK 17 or higher for Antora to build successfully.
Missing JDK Errors Errors like No matching toolchains found for requested specification indicate a missing JDK that needs to be installed.

Documentation is generated in docs/build/site/index.html and in docs/build/distributions/reactor-core-<version>-docs.zip. If a PDF file is included in the generated docs zip, the -PforcePdf option must be specified, which requires the asciidoctor-pdf command to be available in the PATH.

#ReactiveProgramming #Java #JVM #Reactor #ReactiveStreams

Source: reactor/reactor-core

💡 Why it matters

item.title: agent-shell brings AI agents to Emacs with ACP
item.description:
agent-shell brings AI agents to Emacs with ACP

agent-shell brings your favorite AI agents to Emacs, keeping you at home: familiar buffers and bindings, no terminal emulation. All powered by ACP, the Agent Client Protocol. Works with 24 agents today, and any other that speaks ACP.

🔍 Overview

  • agent-shell brings your favorite AI agents to Emacs, keeping you at home: familiar buffers and bindings, no terminal emulation.
  • All powered by ACP, the Agent Client Protocol.
  • Works with 24 agents today, and any other that speaks ACP.

🧩 How it works

  • agent-shell relies on acp.el to communicate with agents via ACP (Agent Client Protocol).
  • We now have a handful of additional packages to extend the agent-shell experience:
    • emacs-skills: Claude Agent skills for Emacs.
    • agent-shell-to-go: Interact with agent-shell sessions from your mobile or any other device via Slack.
    • agent-circus: Run AI coding agents in sandboxed Docker containers.
    • agent-shell-sidebar: A sidebar add-on for agent-shell.
    • agent-shell-bookmark: Bookmark support for agent-shell sessions.
    • agent-shell-workspace: Dedicated tab-bar workspace for managing multiple agent-shell sessions.
    • agent-shell-manager: Tabulated view and management of agent-shell buffers.
    • agent-review: Code review interface for agent-shell.
    • agent-shell-attention.el: Mode-line attention tracker for agent-shell.
    • agent-shell-knockknock: Notifications for agent-shell via knockknock.el.
    • agent-shell-notifications: Desktop notifications for agent-shell events.
    • meta-agent-shell: Multi-agent coordination system for agent-shell with inter-agent communication, task tracking, and project-level dispatching.

⚙️ Key details

  • Run thousands of AI agent sandboxes on the cheapest machines.
  • Sandstorm pauses idle sandboxes and snapshots them to disk, then restores them quickly when a request arrives, so one machine can hold far more sandboxes than it could run at once.
  • It supports two sandbox backends, gVisor containers and Firecracker microVMs.
  • Every sandbox has its own network namespace, and both backends can run in one fleet, each forming a resource pool of its own.
  • The master serves a web console for viewing and managing sandboxes and scheduling across the fleet.
  • Agents spend much of their time waiting.
  • Sandstorm is designed around this behavior, with four sandbox tiers that progressively suspend idle sandboxes and quickly wake them when requests arrive.
  • The master keeps desired state in SQLite and places sandboxes.
  • Nodes join by address and pairing code, or dial out from behind NAT.
  • A gateway on the sandbox’s node wakes it and forwards the request.
  • Nodes refuse new work when memory runs low, so SSH stays reachable.
  • sandstormd serves as the master, node, and web console.
  • gVisor and Firecracker each get their own optimizations.
  • The master’s web console shows sandbox states, tier transitions, and node headroom.
  • Measured 2026-10-31, with requests from each node to its own gateway, so no network is in the path.
  • gVisor needs no KVM and ran on six cloud nodes.
  • Firecracker ran on one machine with KVM and one cloud VM under PVM.
  • The hosts differ, so read each column on its own.
  • Traffic is 40 sandboxes per node with a few getting most requests; about 12 fit awake on a gVisor node.
  • p50 is 6-10 ms on gVisor, 7-50 ms on KVM.

🚀 Availability

  • agent-shell is available with additional packages to extend its functionality.

💡 Why it matters

  • agent-shell brings AI agents to Emacs, providing a familiar and integrated environment for AI interactions.
  • The use of ACP allows for compatibility with a wide range of AI agents.
  • The sandboxing and management features of Sandstorm enable efficient and scalable AI agent operations.

#AIagents #Emacs #ACP #Sandstorm #agent-shell

Source: xenodium/agent-shell Source: deeplethe/sandstorm

Datasette Lite: Browser-Based SQLite Database Explorer

Datasette Lite is a port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. It allows users to browse SQLite databases, JSON files, CSV files, or SQL scripts without needing a full web server.

🔍 Overview

  • Datasette Lite enables browsing of SQLite databases, JSON files, CSV files, or SQL scripts directly in the browser.
  • Users can load specific versions of Datasette from PyPI or specific commits, tags, or branches from the Datasette GitHub repository.
  • Over 100 versions of SQLite are available for use with Datasette.

🧩 How it works

  • Datasette Lite uses service workers to intercept HTTP requests and serve them from client-side code.
  • Each tab has a unique session ID to ensure that requests are routed to the correct Datasette instance.
  • A web worker runs a dedicated Datasette instance for each session.

item.title: GitHub develops Agent Host Protocol to enable continuous multi-device AI sessions
item.description:
GitHub develops Agent Host Protocol to enable continuous multi-device AI sessions

The newly developed Agent Host Protocol (AHP) is an open standard designed to keep AI agent sessions accessible and continuous across editors, applications, mobile phones, and the cloud. As models become capable of working independently for hours or days, AHP ensures that developers can check in on their progress from any device, allowing sessions to persist even when users switch devices or close windows.

🔍 Overview

In the past, GitHub Copilot was built as a VS Code extension, tying the lifetime of agents directly to the VS Code editor window. Closing the window, restarting VS Code for an update, or connecting to a remote machine would terminate the agent session or reset the extension host. To resolve this limitation and allow developers to pull agents into their custom workflows, editors, terminals, or mobile apps, the Agent Host Protocol provides a standard, independently versioned language. This shared protocol ensures every client sees the same agents, history, and state without requiring bespoke, one-off integrations.

🧩 How it works

To handle multi-client interactions seamlessly, the Agent Host Protocol is designed with several core architectural features:

  • URI-identified Channels: This is the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, and can optionally implement other channels such as terminal support, Model Context Protocol (MCP) additions, or OpenTelemetry (OTel) reporting.
  • Reducer-Based State Object: Inside each channel, a reducer-based state object drives client-side logic. The server acts as the arbiter of this state, while the client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects.
  • Network Resiliency: Under poor network conditions, reconnection and replay are simplified. Clients can send all queued actions and present a loading state while waiting for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions.
  • Minimal Core: To make implementation straightforward on custom clients and servers, the core protocol is kept minimal while allowing extensive features to be built on top.

⚙️ Key details

  • Focus on Interaction, Not Behavior: Unlike the Language Server Protocol (LSP) or Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP), AHP avoids encoding how agents work, focusing solely on how users interact with them to accommodate rapidly evolving agent models.
  • Rebuilding the VS Code Stack: Adopting AHP in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The existing Copilot Chat extension had grown for over three years to more than 400,000 lines of TypeScript (excluding tests) and was heavily dependent on the VS Code window lifecycle and APIs that are unavailable in a standalone agent host process.

#AHP #GitHubCopilot #AIAgents #VSCode #DeveloperTools

Source: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices

item.title: Introducing the External Sandbox Pattern for Secure AI Agent Code Execution
item.description:
Introducing the External Sandbox Pattern for Secure AI Agent Code Execution

On November 17, 2026, a new project developed in collaboration with Prime Radiant introduced the external sandbox pattern. Under this pattern, code executed by an AI agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox, while the agent itself resides outside of that sandbox.

🔍 Overview

The external sandbox pattern separates the AI agent from the environment where its executed code runs. To demonstrate this pattern, three sandbox server implementations have been released. These sandboxes can be configured to receive API calls from AI agents such as Pi, Claude Code, or Codex whenever they need to execute code.

⚙️ Key features

  • Unified API: Each implementation offers the same localhost API.
  • Allow-list Proxy: An optional HTTP/HTTPS proxy to control exactly which hosts the agent’s code is allowed to communicate with.
  • Credential Replacement: A mechanism that allows the agent’s code to make authenticated API calls without sharing secret credentials directly with the agent.

🧩 Sandbox implementations

Implementation Description
external-sandbox-v86 A Node.js server that uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
external-sandbox-container A Python web server that runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
external-sandbox-quicksand A Python web server that uses Microsoft’s Quicksand sandboxing library to bundle QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package.

#AIAgents #Sandboxing #PrimeRadiant #SecureCode

Source: External sandboxes for coding agents

item.title: Java4Shell: Critical Vulnerability in OpenJDK
item.description:
Java4Shell: Critical Vulnerability in OpenJDK

On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime.

🔍 Overview

  • Java4Shell is a critical vulnerability with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10.
  • It affects Java applications and can be exploited remotely without credentials.
  • OpenJDK and Oracle released patched builds on the same day.

🧩 How it works

  • The vulnerability allows a remote attacker to send malformed Base64 data to a Java application.
  • This data overwrites memory next to the decoded output, leading to heap memory leaks and remote code execution.
  • The bug is in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input.
  • An invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write, overwriting neighboring memory.

⚙️ Key details

  • Java4Shell can be triggered by a simple input of 64 A characters followed by =.
  • The vulnerability affects various Java applications, including Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, and Jenkins.
  • Base64 is commonly used to represent binary data as text in Java applications.

🚀 Availability

  • Cloudflare has released new rules to detect malformed Base64 input patterns.
  • These rules are available on Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action.
  • Customers can review matching requests and change the rules action to Block.
  • The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch.

💡 Why it matters

  • Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses.
  • The only complete fix is to update the Java runtime.
  • Cloudflare has seen no indication of Java4Shell exploitation on its infrastructure.
  • Analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques appear.

#Java4Shell #OpenJDK #CVSS #Base64 #Security

Source: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)

item.title: Model Context Protocol Registry API Enters v0.1 API Freeze
item.description:
Model Context Protocol Registry API Enters v0.1 API Freeze

The community-driven Model Context Protocol (MCP) registry service has launched in preview and its Registry API (v0.1) has entered an API freeze.

🔍 Overview

  • The MCP registry provides MCP clients with a list of MCP servers, functioning like an app store for MCP servers.
  • The registry has launched in preview with an announcement blog post.
  • While the system is now more stable, this is still a preview release and breaking changes or data resets may occur.
  • A general availability (GA) release will follow later.

⚙️ Key details

  • For the next month or more, the API will remain stable with no breaking changes, allowing integrators to confidently implement support.
  • This freeze applies to v0.1 while development continues on v0.
  • This period will be used to validate the API in real-world integrations and gather feedback to shape v1 for general availability.
  • Publishing an MCP server does not happen through a pull request to the repository; adding a server.json, a server directory, or an entry in data/seed.json will not publish or list your server, even if the PR is merged.
  • Users must use the mcp-publisher CLI from their server’s own project instead.

🚀 Availability

  • The registry uses ko to build container images, and pre-built Docker images are automatically published to GitHub Container Registry.
  • Starting the registry at localhost:8080 with PostgreSQL uses ephemeral storage that resets each time containers are restarted.
  • By default, the registry seeds from the production API with a filtered subset of servers to keep startup fast.
  • The image does not bundle PostgreSQL, so users must run their own and point the registry at it via MCP_REGISTRY_DATABASE_URL.
  • Setup can be configured with environment variables in docker-compose.yml, and .env.example provides a reference.
  • Docker run commands are available for ghcr.io/modelcontextprotocol/registry:latest, :main, :v1.0.0, and :main-20250906-abc123d.

item.title: Optimize Generative AI Costs by Bypassing Model Calls Where Possible
item.description:
Optimize Generative AI Costs by Bypassing Model Calls Where Possible

Teams often route every task through a large language model, including input validation, formatting, and routing. While each call is cheap in isolation, these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture at production scale. This development highlights a pattern for deciding whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all, allowing teams to map options to deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock.

🧩 How it works

The pattern usually starts in a prototype where a model call works for one step and becomes the default for subsequent steps, such as validating input, reformatting a request body, or picking a route. At prototype volume, the cost is unnoticed, but at production volume, unneeded model calls create problems in three ways:

  • Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps.
  • Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Output can vary because the same input can return a different answer, making testing harder and audits slower.

Each new model launch restarts the debate about which model to use, while the question of whether the step needs a model at all goes unasked. Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens, often starts at model selection. This approach starts one step earlier: determining if a model is required.

⚙️ Key details

The decision process involves a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. The following questions help determine the lane for each step:

  • Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range?
  • Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema?
  • Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no?

If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model. If a rule settles part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first. For example, a keyword match on the fast path resolves messages such as “refund”, and the residual goes to the third question. A model can also draft a regular expression that is reviewed and committed to write the rule once.

💡 Why it matters

Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. This methodology allows teams to map each option to AWS, ensuring that deterministic code, constrained decision calls, or right-sized models on Amazon Bedrock are applied appropriately to optimize generative AI systems.

#GenerativeAI #CostOptimization #AWSCloud #MLOps #AmazonBedrock

Source: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Update on Deja-Vu: Local Memory and Cross-Agent Handoff for 48 Coding Agents
item.description:
Update on Deja-Vu: Local Memory and Cross-Agent Handoff for 48 Coding Agents

Deja-vu (deja) has received new updates providing local memory, session search, and cross-agent handoff across 48 coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, and Hermes.

🔍 Overview

  • Supports 48 coding agents that already save every session to disk.
  • Built as a single Go binary featuring 7 hooks and MCP.
  • Indexes all session data locally with zero LLM calls, achieving a 0.7 ms in-process lookup and a ~4% index footprint.
  • Achieves a recall of 97.2% R@5 on LongMemEval-S.

🧩 Features and Commands

  • Interactive terminal search: Running deja with no arguments opens a search across every agent’s history, prioritizing sessions behind uncommitted changes and recent work in the current project.
  • Navigation: Use up and down arrows to pick a session, enter to open at the match, forward slash to search inside a session, square brackets to jump between turns, and Control-s to toggle date or relevance sort (deja search --sort date).
  • Filtering: Filter by agent (e.g., codex:), time (today, yesterday, week, month), or project (in:<project>).
  • Session management: Press r to reopen a session in its native agent, or o to continue it in another agent with its goal, decisions, and open work.
  • Recover deleted chats: Tab switches between the current project, all projects, and Deleted sessions.
  • Command-line tools:
    • deja "jwt refresh token": Lexical plus structural search across all 48 agent stores.
    • deja handoff --to codex: Continue the active session’s goal and state in another agent.
    • deja restore internal/auth/jwt.go: Recover code an agent overwrote before git commit.
    • deja blame internal/auth/jwt.go:42: Trace which agent session wrote or replaced a line.
    • deja audit: Check retention risk, purged chats, and index health across all 48 stores.

⚙️ Performance Benchmarks

  • Recall: 97.2% LongMemEval-S (compared to MemPalace at 96.6% and agentmemory at 95.2%).
  • Token usage: Uses half the tokens of agentmemory on a task the machine had already solved.
  • Speed: Indexing and lookup take 13.6 seconds and 0.7 ms lookup across 19,195 sessions (next of 7 tools took 72 seconds).

🚀 Availability

  • Node.js / npm: npx @vshulcz/deja-vu install --auto (1-step cross-platform install and wire installed agents).
  • Shell script: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vshulcz/deja-vu/main/install.sh | sh && deja install --auto.
  • Homebrew: brew install deja-vu && deja install --auto.

item.title: .NET SDK enables development of applications using the A2A v1.0 protocol
item.description:
.NET SDK enables development of applications using the A2A v1.0 protocol

A new .NET SDK has been released that allows developers to build and host applications following the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, providing a robust implementation of the specification v1.0.

🧩 How it works

The library supports multiple communication methods, allowing agents to interact through message-based or task-based patterns.

  • Agent Capability Discovery: Retrieves agent capabilities and metadata through agent cards.
  • Message-based Communication: Enables direct, stateless messaging with immediate responses.
  • Task-based Communication: Allows for the creation and management of persistent, long-running agent tasks.
  • Streaming Support: Facilitates real-time communication using Server-Sent Events.

⚙️ Key details

The SDK is built to integrate directly with web application stacks and supports multiple protocol bindings.

Component Description
A2AClient Primary client for making A2A requests to agents; supports streaming, non-streaming, and push notifications.
A2ACardResolver Resolves agent card information from A2A-compatible endpoints.
A2AServer Core server handling A2A JSON-RPC requests and coordinating task lifecycle.
IAgentHandler Interface for agents to implement, providing methods for message handling and task cancellation.
TaskUpdater API for emitting task lifecycle events such as start, complete, and fail.
MessageResponder API for sending stateless message replies without task lifecycle management.

All three protocol bindings—JSON-RPC, HTTP+JSON REST, and gRPC—share the same client contract and server pipeline. The gRPC binding is packaged as optional modules to prevent core consumers from being forced to depend on specific gRPC libraries.

🚀 Availability

The library targets .NET 8 and higher and includes built-in extensions for hosting A2A agents within web applications.

  • The v1.0 implementation is available as a NuGet package.
  • A backward-compatible package is available during the transition period.
  • A configuration option allows developers to explicitly request a completed task response when calling v1 servers from v0.3 clients, which helps avoid returning an incomplete initial task snapshot.

#dotnet #AIagents #A2A #softwaredevelopment #protocol

Source: a2aproject/a2a-dotnet

item.title: AgnostUI Local v2 copies UI components into your project for AI readability
item.description:
AgnostUI Local v2 copies UI components into your project for AI readability

AgnostUI Local (v2) is a new CLI-based UI component library that copies components directly into your project at install time. Instead of keeping components hidden inside node_modules, the source code lands directly in your repository, providing full control and native integration with your framework.

🧩 How it works

AgnostUI components are authored as Lit Web Components, a standards-based layer over native Custom Elements. The CLI wraps these components for your specific framework at copy time. By default, components are placed under src/components/ag/, creating a dedicated namespace that keeps AgnosticUI components separate from your own code. This approach ensures that your design system does not fork when your tech stack changes.

🤖 AI and Agent Integration

Because the component source lives locally, it is readable by AI tools such as Cursor, Claude, Copilot, Windsurf, Aider, Gemini, Replit, Kiro, and Antigravity. Every tool sees the raw source, creating a high-fidelity environment for Generative UI and agent-driven interfaces.

  • Reduce Hallucination: Since the LLM reads local files like any other code, it knows exactly what is possible, preventing invented props or APIs.
  • Better Token Efficiency: Using semantic HTML and standard CSS provides clean context, allowing agents to spend fewer tokens to understand the UI for faster, more accurate generations.
  • Agent Skills: AgnosticUI Playbooks act as pre-defined skills, prompting agents to scaffold complex, accessible workflows using local components.

📜 Playbooks and Components

The schema-driven layer ships with three companion documents. AgnosticUI offers Playbooks that demonstrate modular, prompt-driven UI components. These Playbooks support agent-generated UI workflows directly.

Playbook Name Description
Login Form Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Onboarding Wizard Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Discovery Dashboard Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Support Center Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Data Grid Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Blog / Article Reader Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Landing / Marketing Page Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components

💡 Why it matters

AgnostUI Local solves the “Black Box” problem of traditional libraries hidden in node_modules. It is designed as the architecture for the next era of development, characterized as context-aware, framework-agnostic, and AI-ready.

item.title: AI Coding Agent Optimized with TokenEconomizer
item.description:
AI Coding Agent Optimized with TokenEconomizer

TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that reduces waste in AI coding agent sessions by learning from past sessions and adapting to future ones.

🔍 Overview

TokenEconomizer is a plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model.

🧩 How it works

  • The agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model.
  • TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository.
  • Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes.
  • Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use, while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files.
  • Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure.

⚙️ Key details

  • TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents on 277 real bug-fixing tasks.
  • Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable.
  • The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called.

🚀 Availability

TokenEconomizer is available as an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security.

💡 Why it matters

TokenEconomizer reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on.

📊 Evaluation

  • TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9% on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations.
  • The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench.
  • On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower.

📸 Images

  • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/TokenEconomizer-BlogHeroFeature-1400x788-1.jpg

#AIagents #Open-source #Plugin #Optimization

item.title: Argus AI Security Platform Launches with Self-Hosted Multi-Tenant Capabilities
item.description:
Argus AI Security Platform Launches with Self-Hosted Multi-Tenant Capabilities

A new self-hosted, multi-tenant, and MIT-licensed security platform named Argus has been released to watch cloud, identity, code, endpoints, network, and Kubernetes environments.

🔍 Overview

Argus catches attacks at machine speed, investigates them with AI agents, and contains them in seconds. The platform operates offline for air-gapped installs and ensures security data never leaves the user’s hands.

🧩 How it works

  • Nine specialist agents triage, investigate, and hunt using read-only tools.
  • Agents can propose a fix but never execute one; their one write-capable tool creates a pending request.
  • Everything agents read is treated as untrusted data so prompt injections become signals instead of hijacks.
  • Autonomous response playbooks act the moment a detection fires using a catalog of 27 typed actions.
  • Every autonomous feature ships off by default so users can enable autonomy gradually.

⚙️ Key details

  • AI Gateway: Puts OpenAI and Anthropic traffic behind org-held keys, model allowlists, data-loss prevention, prompt-injection flags, and budgets.
  • Shadow-AI Discovery: Finds services used without approval via network, cloud, and SSO telemetry.
  • Canaries: Built for agents with hidden prompt injections, agent rules files, a fake MCP server, and fake LLM API keys.
  • Attack Simulator: Replays eight AI-driven attack scenarios in an isolated sandbox tenant.
  • Pentesting: Autopilot and native autonomous pentesting plan tests and run them through a scope-checked harness.
  • Vulnerability Enrichment: CVE findings are enriched with CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list and EPSS scores, automatically raising severity.

🚀 Availability

  • Deployment options include Docker Compose for pilots, Helm for Kubernetes, and Terraform for AWS and Azure.
  • Encrypted backups run on a schedule and land on disk, S3, or Azure with single-command restore and verification checks.
  • Control mappings for SOC 2, NIST 800-171, and ISO 27001 are included.

#AISecurity #AIAgents #Cybersecurity #DevSecOps #CloudSecurity

item.title: Ax Ships a TypeScript-First, Multi-Language LLM Toolkit
item.description:
Ax Ships a TypeScript-First, Multi-Language LLM Toolkit

Ax is a TypeScript-first development toolkit that ships as @ax-llm/ax. Its shared semantic core is also compiled into generated Python, Java, C++, Go, and Rust libraries.

🔍 Overview

Ax provides typed structured generation, deployment profiles, agents, flows, and optimizers. The TypeScript package is the source implementation and current published package.

🧩 How it works

Signatures for typed structured generation can be written using:

  • A string DSL
  • The fluent f() builder
  • Any Standard Schema v1 validator, including Zod, Valibot, and ArkType

The deployment name selects wire behavior, while the model ID is resolved inside that deployment. Named deployment profiles cover native APIs, routers, hosted inference, configurable runtimes, audio, and realtime event streams.

For example:

1
2
3

const llm = ai({ name: "openai", apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_APIKEY });
const classify = ax('review:string -> sentiment:class "positive, negative, neutral"',);
await classify.forward(llm, { review: "This product is amazing!" })

The evidence describes this example as requiring no prompt engineering. The provider name can be switched from "openai" to "anthropic", "google-gemini", "meta", "together", "fireworks", "deepseek", or "grok", among others.

⚙️ Key details

  • Agents: runtime execution, context budgets, checkpoints, action-log replay, discovery, memory, skills, and delegation.
  • Flows: typed program graphs supporting branches, loops, feedback, cache behavior, parallel execution, and .returns(...) projection.
  • Optimizers: GEPA, few-shot bootstrapping, portable optimizer artifacts, and evaluation/apply flows.
  • Runtime path: Ax is designed to stay in the same latency class as direct provider calls while adding typed outputs, validation, retries, tools, tracing, and memory. Its hot path renders the signature, calls the provider, parses the result, and returns a typed value.
  • Streaming: Streaming is the default. Ax can parse fields as they arrive, run streaming assertions, fail early, cancel an in-flight stream, and start correction.

🚀 Availability

Language Package or distribution Availability
TypeScript / JavaScript @ax-llm/ax Published on npm
Python axllm Published on PyPI
Java dev.axllm:ax Published on Maven Central
C++ axllm::axllm CMake FetchContent source build
Go github.com/ax-llm/ax/packages/go Installable with go get
Rust axllm Published on crates.io

The same signatures, provider mappings, agents, flows, runtime contracts, and optimizers are compiled into verified generated Python, Java, C++, Go, and Rust libraries.

item.title: claude-tap Offers Local Tracing for AI Coding Agents
item.description:
claude-tap Offers Local Tracing for AI Coding Agents

claude-tap is a local proxy and trace viewer for AI coding agents, letting users inspect API traffic and agent context. Its workflow supports reviewing individual requests, comparing changes between turns, and exporting trace sessions as standalone HTML files.

🔍 What it captures

The viewer can show:

  • System prompts and conversation history
  • Tool schemas, tool calls, and tool results
  • Reconstructed streaming responses
  • Token usage
  • Diffs between adjacent requests

Users can run a CLI through claude-tap or listen to local app transcripts, then open an agent run and inspect its requests to see how context changes between turns. The viewer has light and dark modes.

🧩 Supported clients

The evidence lists support for these tools and clients:

  • Claude Code, Codex CLI, Codex App, and Gemini CLI
  • Grok Build CLI, DeepSeek Harness, Kimi CLI, and MiMo Code
  • OpenCode, OpenClaw, Pi, and Hermes Agent
  • Cursor CLI, Qoder CLI, and CodeBuddy CLI

🛠️ Traces and prompt snapshots

Each run writes a local trace session that can be exported as a self-contained HTML viewer for review or archiving. No hosted dashboard is required.

Phistory archives versioned system-prompt snapshots from agent CLIs, including Claude Code, Codex, Kimi, OpenCode, and Pi. It uses claude-tap’s capture-only prompt export to preserve raw HTTP trace evidence and create snapshots for comparison in a prompt diff viewer.

🔐 Data handling

Common authentication headers are replaced with *** before recording, without retaining credential prefixes. Upstream requests receive the original headers. The stated redaction does not cover request or response bodies, URLs, or diagnostic text.

#AIAgents #CodingAgents #DeveloperTools #APIDebugging

DSPyGen is a command-line framework for developing language-model pipelines with DSPy, using a structured, modular approach inspired by Ruby on Rails.

🔍 Overview

DSPyGen is described as a framework for the DSPy project, which works with language models such as GPT, BERT, and Llama. Its stated aim is to simplify creating, developing, and deploying LM pipelines. The project says it was influenced by the work of Sean Chatman and James I. Chatman.

🧩 How it works

The CLI provides commands to initialize a project, generate DSPy modules, run a module, and serve a REST API:

1
2

dspygen init my_project
cd my_project

item.title: Knowhere Provides Milvus’s C++ Vector Search Core
item.description:
Knowhere Provides Milvus’s C++ Vector Search Core

Knowhere is an independent C++ project that serves as Milvus’s internal core for vector search, integrating FAISS, HNSW and DiskANN. It can be built as part of Milvus or developed as a library, with CPU and GPU build options.

🔍 Overview

Knowhere acts as Milvus’s internal vector search engine. For users who want to use it within Milvus without modifying Knowhere’s source code, the project recommends building Milvus directly; Knowhere is then built implicitly.

⚙️ Platforms and dependencies

All Linux distributions are available for Knowhere development. Most contributors work on Ubuntu or CentOS, with a smaller group using Mac systems on x86_64 or Apple Silicon.

The project lists these verified operating systems for building and running Knowhere:

Operating system Details
Ubuntu 22.04 x86_64 and Aarch64
Ubuntu 20.04 x86_64 and Aarch64; kept for legacy reasons, with EOL by April 2025
macOS x86_64 and Apple Silicon

The scripts/install_deps.sh script installs dependencies for building, testing and shipping the Knowhere library.

🖥️ Build options

GPU support is disabled by default. Setting WITH_GPU=True enables Cardinal GPU support when building with Cardinal, or cuVS otherwise. WITH_CUVS=True explicitly enables cuVS, including alongside Cardinal, independently of WITH_GPU.

GPU builds use CUDA 13.2 for both cuVS and Cardinal. CMake prepares the toolkit before enabling CUDA, including when Knowhere is built through add_subdirectory. An existing toolkit at /usr/local/cuda-13.2 is reused. If it is absent, scripts/install_cuda.sh installs it on Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, on x86_64 or Aarch64, and requires root access or passwordless sudo. Other systems must prepare the toolkit at that path beforehand. A GPU device or driver is not needed to compile, and the build must be reconfigured when switching CUDA versions. CPU builds do not invoke the CUDA installer.

Common build commands include:

Build Command
CPU release (default) make
GPU release with cuVS make WITH_GPU=True
GPU release with Cardinal make WITH_CARDINAL=True WITH_GPU=True
CPU with unit tests make WITH_UT=True
CPU unit tests with AddressSanitizer make WITH_UT=True WITH_ASAN=True
GPU with unit tests make WITH_GPU=True WITH_UT=True
Debug build make WITH_DEBUG=True
C ABI and Java JNI bindings with C tests make WITH_JNI=True WITH_C_API_TESTS=True
Custom compiler through a Conan profile make CONAN_PROFILE=clang14

Building a Python wheel requires swig and Python development headers, such as python3-dev on Ubuntu. A portable manylinux wheel can be built with make wheel.

🔌 Bindings and contributions

Optional C ABI and Java 11 JNI bindings expose indexes, brute-force search and named index blobs without a framework dependency. The Java bindings are documented in java/README.md.

Before submitting a pull request, contributors can install and enable pre-commit hooks with pip3 install pre-commit and pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit --hook-type pre-push. They can run all hooks with make pre-commit, or run formatting and linting separately with make format and make lint. The lint command uses clang-tidy and requires a prior build. If clang-format and clang-tidy are not installed, the project provides installation instructions for Linux and Mac.

#Knowhere #Milvus #VectorSearch #C++ #CUDA

Source: zilliztech/knowhere

item.title: Kody Updates Portable Cloud Platform for AI Agent Memory and Automations
item.description:
Kody Updates Portable Cloud Platform for AI Agent Memory and Automations

Kody has introduced new updates to its portable agents’ cloud, designed to manage the memory, keys, code, and automations of AI agents across Model Context Protocol (MCP) hosts. Built on Cloudflare Workers, this source-available platform supports both individuals and teams by providing account isolation and a flexible development environment.

🔍 Overview

Kody provides an MCP-first architecture intended to work across compatible AI agent hosts, with ChatGPT serving as a likely primary host target. Rather than functioning as a general-purpose agent harness, Kody focuses on enabling portability for an agent’s critical assets. Each account on the platform represents an isolated environment holding its own packages, jobs, credentials, memories, and related state. To maintain security, no account is given privileged status at runtime.

🧩 How it works

Instead of managing a large, static tool catalog, Kody prioritizes a compact MCP surface area designed around powerful flows. Key behaviors and request flows include:

  • Flow Preferences: The platform favors powerful search and Code Mode execute flows.
  • Request Ordering: OAuth requests are processed first, followed by MCP requests, and finally static assets.
  • Webhook Processing: Webhook ingress, including GET subscription challenges, is handled in the Worker fetch path before being routed to TanStack Start.
  • Web Application: The remaining website requests are routed through TanStack Start at packages/worker/start/http-entry.ts.
  • Client Assets: Assets are bundled into packages/worker/public/ and served via the ASSETS binding.

⚙️ Key details

The project utilizes an Nx monorepo structure following several epicflare starter conventions. Shared modules and worker roles are organized as follows:

Module / Package Path Description / Role
packages/shared (@kody-internal/shared) Shared modules used across the repository
packages/worker The origin app worker, with its entrypoint at packages/worker/src/index.ts
packages/platform-worker Sibling worker managing platform services
packages/runtime-worker Sibling worker managing runtime tasks
packages/jobs-worker Sibling worker managing automated jobs
packages/mock-servers/* Mock Workers for local testing and simulation

For contributors getting started with development, the local dev server runs on localhost:3742 by default. The command-line interface automatically selects the next free port if that one is occupied, and Wrangler manages both the local Cloudflare Workers runtime and the D1 database automatically. Developers and agents can refer to AGENTS.md for repository-specific guidelines, while docs/contributing/project-intent.md explains the core intent of the repository.

#Kody #ModelContextProtocol #CloudflareWorkers #AIAgents #Monorepo
